10: - Use its headed Chromium, persistent Xvfb display, and SwiftShader configuration.
11: - Run `playwright-cli open http://localhost:3002` for the Pascal development server.

const storyBeats=[ {date:'GOTHAM CITY · 1982',title:'A night at the movies',text:'

Gotham’s old theater empties into a rain-bright street. Thomas and Martha Wayne walk home with their young son, Bruce, still talking about the film. His mother holds his hand; his father listens as if the story matters as much as the night is beautiful.

Their shortcut passes a narrow alley. A stranger steps from the dark and asks for money. Thomas does not reach for a weapon or shout. He gives the gunman $200—everything he has—and tries to make himself the only danger in the alley.

“Take it. Just let my family go.”

For one suspended second, the city seems to hold its breath.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM CITY · THAT NIGHT',title:'The promise',text:'

The gunshot cracks across the street. Thomas and Martha fall beneath the streetlamp. Bruce is left kneeling beside them, surrounded by a city that keeps moving but will never look the same to him again.

In the weeks that follow, adults speak softly around him. They tell him he is safe now, that the police will find the killer, that time will make the pain smaller. None of those words can bring his parents back. Bruce learns that helplessness can feel louder than any siren.

Grief hardens into a promise—not a plan yet, only a vow he will carry into every room: no one else should have to feel this alone.

'}, {date:'WAYNE MANOR · THE YEARS AFTER',title:'A house full of echoes',text:'

The manor is enormous, but after the funeral it feels too quiet. Bruce grows up among portraits, locked rooms, and the careful kindness of the family’s longtime butler, Alfred Pennyworth. Alfred makes breakfast, remembers birthdays, and never asks Bruce to pretend he is all right.

Bruce studies, travels, and searches for a way to understand the violence that took his parents. He learns how fear works, how people survive, and how easily a powerful family can mistake its own comfort for the health of its city.

The promise stays with him. It changes shape as he does: first a child’s wish, then a question, and finally a responsibility he cannot hand to anyone else.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM CITY · 2008',title:'A fortune, a house, a name',text:'

Twenty-six years later, Bruce uncovers a fortune his father had quietly set aside—seed money for a plan Thomas never finished. Bruce invests it, buys back a neglected mansion, and gives the work a public name: Wayne Enterprises.

From the outside, it looks like a return to the life he was born to lead. The grand rooms fill with donors, champagne, and polished promises. Harvey Dent, Gotham’s tireless district attorney, is among the guests. He believes the city can be repaired through courage and honest institutions.

Bruce admires that conviction. He also knows how many people are waiting for someone else to fix things. Behind the parties, he begins asking harder questions about what a single person can do.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM CITY · 2009',title:'The cost of hope',text:'

A year later, a terrible incident leaves Harvey Dent’s face scarred and his life changed. The city’s bright public hope is suddenly vulnerable to pain, anger, and the cruel appetite of headlines. Bruce watches the damage from a distance and recognizes the same old feeling: the moment when safety proves it was never guaranteed.

He retreats from the parties and the easy explanations. With a bag in hand, he descends beneath Wayne Manor into a forgotten cave. The stone is cold, the passages are rough, and the darkness seems almost honest. Here, at least, nobody asks him to smile for a photograph.

For a while, Bruce tells himself solitude is the same thing as purpose.

'}, {date:'WAYNE CAVE · THE FIRST VISIT',title:'A man in the dark',text:'

“Excuse me, sir. Are you looking for something?” an old man calls from the cave entrance. “There’s nothing in here. It’s old—just like me.”

Bruce bristles. “I’m trying to do something with this place. What makes you think you can tell me what to do?” The stranger does not rise to the challenge. He simply points out that Bruce is standing on private property and waits for him to answer.

Bruce refuses to leave. The old man gives him one last look and walks away. The exchange is awkward, almost absurd, but it stays with Bruce. Someone has finally spoken to him plainly, without fear of his name or his money.

'}, {date:'WAYNE CAVE · THREE MONTHS LATER',title:'The long quiet',text:'

Days pass. Bruce returns to the cave with tools, then with plans, then with nothing but questions. He measures the cavern and marks out possible work areas. He tries to turn the rock into a headquarters by force of will, but every task exposes another one he does not know how to do.

Above him, the manor continues its routines. Below, the cave answers with drips of water and the occasional flutter of wings. Bruce begins to understand that a mission built alone may only become another way to hide.

One evening he hears footsteps at the entrance. The same old man has come back. This time, he is carrying a thermos and a small stack of notes.

'}, {date:'WAYNE CAVE · A RETURN',title:'An unexpected ally',text:'

“Excuse me, sir. Remember me?” The man sets down the thermos. “I’m Alfred.” Bruce has known him all his life, of course, but down here they meet differently: not as employer and servant, nor as grieving boy and patient guardian, but as two people looking at the same unfinished room.

Alfred has sketched a workbench, a computer station, and a safer route back to the house. He has also found a book on self-defense. Bruce studies the pages and recognizes how much he does not know. Alfred does not gloat. He pours tea.

“You’ll need more than determination, sir,” he says. “Determination is what gets you to the door. Preparation is what gets you home.”

'}, {date:'WAYNE CAVE · THE PLAN TAKES SHAPE',title:'Tools, not answers',text:'

They work in fits and starts. Alfred knows how to keep a project moving; Bruce knows how to ask questions that make the project bigger. The computer station becomes a place to sort reports and maps. A suit bay takes shape against the stone. The elevator connects the cave to the estate without sending either man through the front hall.

Every object has a purpose and a limit. Batarangs can distract or disarm, but they cannot make a bad decision wise. Smoke pellets can cover a retreat, but they cannot turn a retreat into a victory. A grapple prototype can bridge a gap only if the person using it thinks before leaping.

Bruce begins to see the cave not as a lair, but as a workshop for learning how to help.

'}, {date:'WAYNE CAVE · THE VEHICLE BAY',title:'A machine with sharp edges',text:'

The car is the most ambitious piece of the plan and the least finished. Its armored panels catch the work lights; its engine answers a test with a growl that makes dust fall from the ceiling. Alfred circles it with a clipboard, noting what still needs attention.

“It’s not quite street legal,” he says. “And I would avoid the red switch.” Bruce asks if it is safe. Alfred considers the question for a beat too long. They agree to call it a prototype and to keep the first test somewhere far from traffic.

The machine represents possibility, but also temptation: the urge to make an entrance instead of doing the patient work. Bruce closes the hood. Tonight, the car can wait.

'}, {date:'WAYNE CAVE · BEFORE DAWN',title:'The first lesson',text:'

Alfred lays the self-defense field guide on the workbench. It is not as impressive as the suit, the car, or the glowing computer screens. Its pages are worn at the corners, full of diagrams and notes in Alfred’s neat hand. Bruce opens it carefully.

“Begin with the book,” Alfred tells him. “Learn how to keep your balance. Learn when to move, when to listen, and when walking away is the bravest thing you can do.” Bruce looks toward the equipment waiting around the cave. For the first time, it feels less like a collection of answers and more like a list of responsibilities.

There is still a long way to go. But the work has finally begun.

'}, {date:'WAYNE CAVE · NOW',title:'A place to begin',text:'

Alfred has left the gear ready: the field guide on the bench, prototypes on the armor table, the suit in its display frame, and the Batmobile resting beneath the stone ceiling. The elevator waits at the far end of the cave. Nothing here is finished, and nobody pretends otherwise.

Bruce takes in the quiet workshop and the steady lights. Beyond the cave lies a city full of strangers, each with a story he cannot know yet. He cannot undo the night that changed his life. He can choose what he does with the nights still ahead.

One man. One promise. A first step into the dark.

Explore the cave, inspect every piece of equipment, and take the elevator when you are ready.

## Requirements
- Build or modify the playable game without asking clarifying questions.
- Make the story long.
- Save verification screenshots as JPEGs no wider than 1280px, and inspect only the latest screenshot.

## Decisions
- Increased movement speed and allowed keyboard movement during dialogue.
- Expanded the intro story from 6 to 11 detailed beats.
- Made the story card scrollable and improved touch-control visibility.

## Work State
### Completed
- Updated `index.html` with the longer story, stronger movement, keyboard input handling, and responsive story/touch-control styling.
- Extracted the module JavaScript and passed `node --check`.
- Opened the game in Playwright.

### Active
- Verify walking, story progression, and controls in-browser.
- Capture and inspect a current small JPEG screenshot.

### Blocked
- Browser gameplay and visual appearance have not yet been confirmed.

## Next Move
1. Continue browser testing at `http://localhost:3002`; start the story and confirm keyboard/touch movement and interactions.
2. Save a JPEG screenshot at a viewport no wider than 1280px and inspect only that latest image.
3. Review any remaining console warnings and address issues if needed.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Game code and current changes; uncommitted.

## Important Context
- Playwright reported a missing `/favicon.ico` (404); no other console errors were reported.

In the weeks that follow, adults speak softly around him. They tell him he is safe now, that the police will find the killer, that time will make the pain smaller. None of those words can bring his parents back. Bruce learns that helplessness can feel louder than any siren.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM CITY · 2009',title:'The cost of hope',text:'

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 01',title:'The first patrol',text:'

At 02:14, Bruce leaves the cave wearing the unfinished suit. The city is wet, violent, and divided into islands of light. Alfred watches on the radio, correcting course without pretending to know the way.

Bruce stops a mugging near Crime Alley. The victim asks why a masked man would help. “Because the city was not enough to save my parents,” Bruce answers, then immediately realizes that is not the whole truth.

He heads home before dawn. Alfred: “You survived. Tomorrow, we improve the plan.”

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 02',title:'The Red Triangle',text:'

A traveling circus van appears in four simultaneous theft reports. Children call the masked thieves acrobats. Alfred calls them organized. Batman calls them a warning.

A red-winged emblem on a crate leads to the Penguin. Oswald Cobblepot is buying old sewer access, waterfront property, and the loyalty of Gotham’s hungry.

Batman closes the first vault, but Cobblepot escapes into the neglected flood tunnels below the East End.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 04',title:'Riddles in rain',text:'

Green question marks appear across public records. The Riddler, Edward Nygma, claims Gotham’s hidden systems are puzzles waiting for a clever hand.

Every riddle names a witness. One points to Dent. Another points to Wayne Enterprises. Batman begins learning the difference between being mocked and being asked a question.

The latest challenge leads to the clocktower and a trap that nearly buries the Batmobile beneath glass and steel.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 06',title:'The tea invitation',text:'

Poison Ivy has sealed an abandoned greenhouse beneath Robinson Park. Police drones wilt at the glass. Inside, Jervis Tetch—the Mad Hatter—hosts a tea party for captives whose memories have been distorted by a mind-control device.

Ivy offers Batman a bargain: expose Wayne Enterprises’ toxic contracts, and she will let the hostages go. He refuses to bargain with hostages, but accepts a smaller truth—Gotham poisoned the soil long before Ivy began fighting for it.

The tea party ends, though Tetch slips away through a rabbit-sized maintenance door.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 08',title:'Killer Croc below',text:'

During a subway evacuation, Killer Croc overturns a construction train. Batman finds the panic is real but the attack is scripted: the train is carrying stolen medical serum for Bane.

Croc could have escaped. Instead he remains to protect trapped maintenance workers. Batman recognizes manipulation, but not enough to release Croc without judgment.

Alfred extracts the men. Croc disappears into the old canal beneath the city, leaving only a warning: “He knows where you sleep.”

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 10',title:'Red Hood',text:'

The Batcomputer identifies an unauthorized vigilante using a red hood and brutal methods. Witnesses call him Jason Todd. The name reaches Bruce before the evidence does.

Jason confronts Batman with a list of criminals he believes Batman is protecting by restraint. Their argument becomes a pursuit over the Narrows rooftops. Jason is faster, angrier, and far less afraid to fall.

Batman loses sight of him. Alfred reminds Bruce that refusing to become a killer does not mean he can ignore a former student in pain.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 12',title:'The laughing dossier',text:'

The Joker infiltrates Gotham General disguised as an orderly. No one agrees on his motive because no one agrees on the crime: he steals blood, a child’s birthday card, and a list of sealed witnesses.

Batman enters the hospital in a silence of IV pumps and humming machines. Joker leaves a riddle: “A city is a joke only when everyone forgets the punchline.”

Commissioner Gordon finds Batman at the emergency stairwell. Together they realize the seemingly random incidents form a map.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 14',title:'Beneath the courthouse',text:'

The villains’ crimes point toward a buried transit station beneath Gotham’s old courthouse. Bane controls it, but he has not moved against Batman directly.

He has assembled the city’s broken agents and given each one a customized target. He calls it the Twenty-Four, because Gotham, in his view, has been warned for too long.

Batman sees the larger plan: overwhelm the night, isolate Gordon, turn every hero into evidence, and then reveal an exhausted city.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 16',title:'Two-Face’s choice',text:'

Two-Face takes control of the abandoned 1st National vault. His decisions are determined by a scarred coin, but his speeches are never left to chance.

He offers Batman a seat in judgment: save one district attorney or one innocent witness. Batman instead saves both, but Dent refuses to recognize a victory without a rule.

Before he leaves, Dent warns Bruce that justice built on luck is still only fear wearing a uniform.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 18',title:'The plant underground',text:'

Ivy turns Gotham’s pumping stations green. Trees break through asphalt and vines pull at the sewer gates. The transformation could flood half the East End, but Ivy insists it is a quarantine.

Batman learns Wayne Enterprises used the aquifer for unauthorized waste storage. He cannot deny the evidence. He promises to open every record and resign his public defenses.

Ivy releases the city from its flood, on the condition that Alfred, not a corporation, manages the first cleanup.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 20',title:'Cobblepot’s shadow',text:'

The Penguin activates his waterline fleet. Armed umbrellas become alarms and submarines masquerade as municipal barges. Cobblepot intends to make Gotham physically dependent on his monopoly.

Batman dismantles the barges with a blackout, then risks capture to stop a worker trapped below deck. Cobblepot is impressed by the rescue and angry because it undermines his story.Jervis Tetch broadcasts a hypnotic children’s broadcast across Gotham. Everyone who watches begins to repeat nursery rhymes and forget recent hours.

Batman and Gordon use a dead analog signal to reach the city’s radio engineers. Alfred reconstructs Tetch’s command pattern from a field of nonsense.

The broadcast ends. Tetch is arrested smiling, but he has not revealed the four-hour gap Bane required.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 24',title:'The war in the halfway house',text:'

Jason Todd ambushes two rival gangs carrying Bane’s serum. One gang member recognizes Jason and calls him Robin, though Jason rejects the name. Batman finds the boy beneath the red hood just as Bane’s scouts arrive.

Bane breaks through the ceiling and defeats Batman with precise, economical force. Jason saves him, not out of forgiveness, but because Bane did not grant anyone a choice.

For the first time, Batman understands Jason may be his ally rather than his opposite.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 26',title:'A board vote',text:'

Lucius Fox brings Bruce evidence of a Wayne Enterprises board plot. The villains have bought influence through companies hidden behind the aquifer scandal.

Bruce returns to a boardroom, shedding the Batman persona instead of hiding behind it. He releases the corruption files, cancels the failed programs, and offers the workers amnesty for testimony.

It is a political victory—and a public target. Joker sends Bruce a photograph of Wayne Manor with the lights still on.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 28',title:'Killer Croc in daylight',text:'

Killer Croc emerges from the canal to deliver Bane’s ledger to Gordon. He was never loyal to Bane; he was protecting a colony of sewer workers forced into labor.

Batman has to decide whether to arrest Croc or accept his evidence. Gordon gives the decision to Croc’s people. They choose the witness interview.

Alfred calls it a legal inconvenience. Bruce calls it the beginning of a neighborhood becoming visible.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 30',title:'The trap in the sky',text:'

Nygma takes control of the GCPD light grid and paints questions across Gotham’s clouds. Each correct answer disables a bomb. The puzzle is not in logic but in sacrifice: each answer protects a district he has already abandoned.

Batman realizes Nygma expects him to save the district where Wayne Enterprises began. He chooses the poorest district instead. The explosives expose a hidden tunnel rather than a skyline.

Nygma escapes into Arkham’s east wing, laughing that Batman solved the wrong problem first.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 32',title:'Arkham without walls',text:'

Arkham’s east wing is opened, not breached. Two-Face, Joker, Ivy, Nygma, and Cobblepot have their own exits. Bane planned to give Gotham a choice: submit or chase.

Batman refuses to pursue every criminal at once. Gordon organizes the city, Jason handles one street gang, and Ivy frees the patients from Tetch’s signal.

The first true alliance begins without costumes or speeches. Alfred arranges for coffee and batteries.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 34',title:'The coin falls',text:'

Two-Face arrives in the Arkham chapel. Dent demands a final vote on Batman’s future. Gordon produces evidence that Dent was manipulated as carefully as every other villain.

For once, Dent cannot blame chance. He flips the coin and refuses the result, splitting it across the chapel floor.

Batman and Gordon escort him to trial. Two-Face looks almost relieved to be answered by a law he can challenge rather than a chance that cannot hear him.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 36',title:'The Lazarus engine',text:'

Bane activates machinery beneath Gotham to flood the storm drains and isolate the Narrows. His goal is not destruction; it is to force Batman to choose between the wealthy and the poor.

Batman shuts down the engine from three locations, aided by the criminals who now know Bane lied to them. Croc removes a jammed gate. Ivy restores the plant relays. Jason saves the control team.

Bane remains in the center of the storm, waiting for Batman to become afraid enough to fight alone.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 38',title:'The silent promise',text:'

Joker has rigged Wayne Manor’s cave elevator with a trap. Batman enters believing Alfred is trapped inside. Instead Alfred is still at the manor, guiding a civilian evacuation.

The Joker appears on every monitor. “No mask,” he says, “no miracle.” Batman answers in Bruce Wayne’s voice and says there is no miracle, only a team that can survive the next minute.

Joker loses interest in a man who cannot be reduced to a single reaction. He escapes toward Bane’s citadel.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 39',title:'The last enemy',text:'

Bane offers Batman the city in exchange for surrendering the Batcave. All Gotham must do is kneel, Bane says, and he will stop breaking it.

Batman refuses. Alfred, Gordon, Jason, Fox, Croc, Ivy, Dent, and the Penguin’s former workers link into a plan spanning streets, towers, tunnels, and servers.

Bane calls them a crowd. Batman calls them Gotham.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 40',title:'Forty hours until dawn',text:'

At the end of forty hours, Batman faces Bane above the flooded central square. He does not win because he is stronger. He wins because he has made preparation out of every painful lesson.

Jason prevents a collapse. Gordon opens the escape routes. Ivy disables the venom pumps. Croc removes Bane’s final supports. Dent and Cobblepot choose their own codes of justice. Joker, Nygma, and Tetch are confined where they can no longer direct the city.

Dawn reaches Wayne Tower. Bruce watches with Alfred and knows the promise is not a promise to end fear. It is a promise to keep working until every frightened person can come home.

The first night became forty hours. Gotham remained. So did the work.

'}, {date:'WAYNE CAVE · NOW',title:'A place to begin',text:'

Alfred has left the gear ready: the field guide on the bench, prototypes on the armor table, the suit in its display frame, and the Batmobile resting beneath the stone ceiling. The elevator waits at the far end of the cave.

Bruce takes in the quiet workshop and the steady lights. Beyond the cave lies a city full of strangers, and a forty-hour story that will shape the Batman he becomes. He cannot undo the night that changed his life, but he can choose what he does with the nights ahead.

One man. One promise. One team. A first step into the dark.

Explore the cave, inspect every piece of equipment, and take the elevator when you are ready.

{date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 01',title:'The first patrol',text:'

At 02:14, Bruce leaves the cave in the unfinished suit. The city is wet, violent, and divided into islands of light. Alfred watches on the radio, correcting course without pretending to know the way.

Bruce stops a mugging near Crime Alley. The victim asks why a masked man would help. Bruce answers that the city was not enough to save his parents, then recognizes that this is not the whole truth.

He returns before dawn. Alfred: “You survived. Tomorrow, we improve the plan.”

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 02',title:'The Red Triangle',text:'

A traveling circus van appears in four simultaneous theft reports. Children call the masked thieves acrobats. Alfred calls them organized. Batman calls them a warning.

A red-winged emblem leads to the Penguin. Oswald Cobblepot is buying sewer access, waterfront property, and the loyalty of Gotham’s hungry.

Batman closes the first vault, but Cobblepot escapes into the neglected flood tunnels beneath the East End.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 04',title:'Riddles in rain',text:'

Green question marks appear across public records. The Riddler, Edward Nygma, claims Gotham’s hidden systems are puzzles waiting for a clever hand.

Every riddle names a witness. One points to Dent. Another points to Wayne Enterprises. Batman learns the difference between being mocked and being asked a question.

The latest challenge leads to the clocktower and a trap that nearly buries the Batmobile beneath glass and steel.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 06',title:'The tea invitation',text:'

Poison Ivy has sealed an abandoned greenhouse beneath Robinson Park. Police drones wilt at the glass. Inside, Jervis Tetch—the Mad Hatter—hosts a tea party for captives whose memories have been altered by a mind-control device.

Ivy offers Batman a bargain: expose Wayne Enterprises’ toxic contracts, and she will free the hostages. He refuses to bargain with hostages, but accepts a smaller truth—Gotham poisoned the soil long before Ivy began fighting for it.

The tea party ends, though Tetch slips away through a maintenance door.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 08',title:'Killer Croc below',text:'

During a subway evacuation, Killer Croc overturns a construction train. Batman finds the panic is real but the attack is scripted: the train carries stolen medical serum for Bane.

Croc could have escaped. Instead he remains to protect trapped maintenance workers. Batman recognizes manipulation, but not enough to release Croc without judgment.

Alfred extracts the workers. Croc disappears below the city, leaving a warning: “He knows where you sleep.”

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 10',title:'Red Hood',text:'

The Batcomputer identifies an unauthorized vigilante using a red hood and brutal methods. Witnesses call him Jason Todd. The name reaches Bruce before the evidence does.

Jason confronts Batman with a list of criminals he believes Batman is protecting by restraint. Their argument becomes a pursuit over the Narrows rooftops. Jason is faster, angrier, and less afraid to fall.

Batman loses sight of him. Alfred reminds Bruce that refusing to become a killer does not mean ignoring a former student in pain.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 12',title:'The laughing dossier',text:'

The Joker infiltrates Gotham General disguised as an orderly. No one agrees on his motive because no one agrees on the crime: he steals blood, a birthday card, and a list of sealed witnesses.

Batman enters the hospital in a silence of IV pumps and humming machines. Joker leaves a riddle: “A city is a joke only when everyone forgets the punchline.”

Gordon finds Batman at the emergency stairwell. Together they realize the random incidents form a map.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 14',title:'Beneath the courthouse',text:'

The villains’ crimes point toward a buried transit station beneath Gotham’s old courthouse. Bane controls it, but he has not moved against Batman directly.

He has assembled the city’s broken agents and given each a customized target. He calls it the Twenty-Four, because Gotham has been warned for too long.

Batman sees the larger plan: overwhelm the night, isolate Gordon, turn every hero into evidence, and reveal an exhausted city.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 16',title:'Two-Face’s choice',text:'

Two-Face takes control of the abandoned 1st National vault. His decisions are determined by a scarred coin, but his speeches are never left to chance.

He offers Batman a seat in judgment: save one district attorney or one innocent witness. Batman instead saves both, but Dent refuses to recognize a victory without a rule.

Before he leaves, Dent warns Bruce that justice built on luck is still only fear wearing a uniform.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 18',title:'The plant underground',text:'

Ivy turns Gotham’s pumping stations green. Trees break through asphalt and vines pull at sewer gates. The transformation could flood half the East End, but Ivy insists it is a quarantine.

Batman learns Wayne Enterprises used the aquifer for unauthorized waste storage. He cannot deny the evidence. He promises to open every record and resign his public defenses.

Ivy releases the city from the flood, on the condition that Alfred, not a corporation, manage the first cleanup.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 20',title:'Cobblepot’s shadow',text:'

The Penguin activates his waterline fleet. Armed umbrellas become alarms and submarines masquerade as municipal barges. Cobblepot intends to make Gotham physically dependent on his monopoly.

Batman dismantles the barges with a blackout, then risks capture to stop a worker trapped below deck. Cobblepot is impressed and angry because the rescue undermines his story.

For the first time, the villain offers Batman a truce—of convenience.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 22',title:'The Mad Hatter’s signal',text:'

Jervis Tetch broadcasts a hypnotic children’s program across Gotham. Everyone who watches begins repeating nursery rhymes and forgetting recent hours.

Batman and Gordon use a dead analog signal to reach the city’s radio engineers. Alfred reconstructs Tetch’s command pattern from a field of nonsense.

The broadcast ends. Tetch is arrested smiling, but he has not revealed the four-hour gap Bane required.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 24',title:'The war in the halfway house',text:'

Jason Todd ambushes two rival gangs carrying Bane’s serum. One gang member recognizes Jason and calls him Robin, though Jason rejects the name. Batman finds the boy beneath the red hood just as Bane’s scouts arrive.

Bane breaks through the ceiling and defeats Batman with precise force. Jason saves him, not out of forgiveness, but because Bane did not grant anyone a choice.

For the first time, Batman understands Jason may be his ally rather than his opposite.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 26',title:'A board vote',text:'

Lucius Fox brings Bruce evidence of a Wayne Enterprises board plot. The villains have bought influence through companies hidden behind the aquifer scandal.

Bruce returns to a boardroom, shedding the Batman persona instead of hiding behind it. He releases the corruption files, cancels failed programs, and offers workers amnesty for testimony.

It is a political victory—and a public target. Joker sends Bruce a photograph of Wayne Manor with the lights still on.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 28',title:'Killer Croc in daylight',text:'

Killer Croc emerges from the canal to deliver Bane’s ledger to Gordon. He was never loyal to Bane; he was protecting sewer workers forced into labor.

Batman must decide whether to arrest Croc or accept his evidence. Gordon gives the decision to Croc’s people. They choose the witness interview.

Alfred calls it a legal inconvenience. Bruce calls it the beginning of a neighborhood becoming visible.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 30',title:'The trap in the sky',text:'

Nygma takes control of the GCPD light grid and paints questions across Gotham’s clouds. Each correct answer disables a bomb. The puzzle is not in logic but in sacrifice: each answer protects a district he has already abandoned.

Batman realizes Nygma expects him to save the district where Wayne Enterprises began. He chooses the poorest district instead. The explosives expose a hidden tunnel rather than a skyline.

Nygma escapes into Arkham’s east wing, laughing that Batman solved the wrong problem first.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 32',title:'Arkham without walls',text:'

Arkham’s east wing is opened, not breached. Two-Face, Joker, Ivy, Nygma, and Cobblepot have their own exits. Bane planned to give Gotham a choice: submit or chase.

Batman refuses to pursue every criminal at once. Gordon organizes the city, Jason handles one street gang, and Ivy frees patients from Tetch’s signal.

The first true alliance begins without costumes or speeches. Alfred arranges for coffee and batteries.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 34',title:'The coin falls',text:'

Two-Face arrives in the Arkham chapel. Dent demands a final vote on Batman’s future. Gordon presents evidence that Dent was manipulated as carefully as every other villain.

For once, Dent cannot blame chance. He flips the coin and refuses the result, splitting it across the chapel floor.

Batman and Gordon escort him to trial. Dent looks almost relieved to be answered by a law he can challenge rather than chance that cannot hear him.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 36',title:'The Lazarus engine',text:'

Bane activates machinery beneath Gotham to flood the storm drains and isolate the Narrows. His goal is not destruction; it is to force Batman to choose between the wealthy and the poor.

Batman shuts down the engine from three locations, aided by the criminals who now know Bane lied to them. Croc removes a jammed gate. Ivy restores the plant relays. Jason saves the control team.

Bane remains in the center of the storm, waiting for Batman to become afraid enough to fight alone.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 38',title:'The silent promise',text:'

Joker has rigged Wayne Manor’s cave elevator with a trap. Batman enters believing Alfred is trapped inside. Instead Alfred is still at the manor, guiding a civilian evacuation.

The Joker appears on every monitor. “No mask,” he says, “no miracle.” Batman answers in Bruce Wayne’s voice: there is no miracle, only a team that can survive the next minute.

Joker loses interest in a man who cannot be reduced to a single reaction. He escapes toward Bane’s citadel.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 39',title:'The last enemy',text:'

Bane offers Batman the city in exchange for surrendering the Batcave. All Gotham must do is kneel, Bane says, and he will stop breaking it.

Batman refuses. Alfred, Gordon, Jason, Fox, Croc, Ivy, Dent, and the Penguin’s former workers link into a plan spanning streets, towers, tunnels, and servers.

Bane calls them a crowd. Batman calls them Gotham.

'}, {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 40',title:'Forty hours until dawn',text:'

At the end of forty hours, Batman faces Bane above the flooded central square. He does not win because he is stronger. He wins because preparation has turned every lesson into a choice.

Jason prevents a collapse. Gordon opens the escape routes. Ivy disables the venom pumps. Croc removes Bane’s final supports. Dent and Cobblepot choose their own codes of justice. Joker, Nygma, and Tetch are confined where they cannot direct the city.

Dawn reaches Wayne Tower. Bruce watches with Alfred and knows the promise is not to end fear. It is to keep working until every frightened person can come home.

The first night became forty hours. Gotham remained. So did the work.

'}, {date:'WAYNE CAVE · NOW',title:'A place to begin',text:'

Alfred has left the gear ready: the field guide on the bench, prototypes on the armor table, the suit in its display frame, and the Batmobile resting beneath the stone ceiling. The elevator waits at the far end of the cave.

Bruce takes in the quiet workshop and the steady lights. Beyond the cave lies a city full of strangers, and a forty-hour story that will shape the Batman he becomes. He cannot undo the night that changed his life, but he can choose what he does with the nights ahead.

One man. One promise. One team. A first step into the dark.

Explore the cave, inspect every piece of equipment, and take the elevator when you are ready.

'} ];let beat=0;

Index: index.html =================================================================== --- index.html +++ index.html @@ -108,9 +108,31 @@ {date:'WAYNE CAVE · A RETURN',title:'An unexpected ally',text:'

“Excuse me, sir. Remember me?” The man sets down the thermos. “I’m Alfred.” Bruce has known him all his life, of course, but down here they meet differently: not as employer and servant, nor as grieving boy and patient guardian, but as two people looking at the same unfinished room.

Alfred has sketched a workbench, a computer station, and a safer route back to the house. He has also found a book on self-defense. Bruce studies the pages and recognizes how much he does not know. Alfred does not gloat. He pours tea.

“You’ll need more than determination, sir,” he says. “Determination is what gets you to the door. Preparation is what gets you home.”

'}, {date:'WAYNE CAVE · THE PLAN TAKES SHAPE',title:'Tools, not answers',text:'

They work in fits and starts. Alfred knows how to keep a project moving; Bruce knows how to ask questions that make the project bigger. The computer station becomes a place to sort reports and maps. A suit bay takes shape against the stone. The elevator connects the cave to the estate without sending either man through the front hall.

Every object has a purpose and a limit. Batarangs can distract or disarm, but they cannot make a bad decision wise. Smoke pellets can cover a retreat, but they cannot turn a retreat into a victory. A grapple prototype can bridge a gap only if the person using it thinks before leaping.

Bruce begins to see the cave not as a lair, but as a workshop for learning how to help.

'}, {date:'WAYNE CAVE · THE VEHICLE BAY',title:'A machine with sharp edges',text:'

The car is the most ambitious piece of the plan and the least finished. Its armored panels catch the work lights; its engine answers a test with a growl that makes dust fall from the ceiling. Alfred circles it with a clipboard, noting what still needs attention.

“It’s not quite street legal,” he says. “And I would avoid the red switch.” Bruce asks if it is safe. Alfred considers the question for a beat too long. They agree to call it a prototype and to keep the first test somewhere far from traffic.

The machine represents possibility, but also temptation: the urge to make an entrance instead of doing the patient work. Bruce closes the hood. Tonight, the car can wait.

'}, {date:'WAYNE CAVE · BEFORE DAWN',title:'The first lesson',text:'

Alfred lays the self-defense field guide on the workbench. It is not as impressive as the suit, the car, or the glowing computer screens. Its pages are worn at the corners, full of diagrams and notes in Alfred’s neat hand. Bruce opens it carefully.

“Begin with the book,” Alfred tells him. “Learn how to keep your balance. Learn when to move, when to listen, and when walking away is the bravest thing you can do.” Bruce looks toward the equipment waiting around the cave. For the first time, it feels less like a collection of answers and more like a list of responsibilities.

There is still a long way to go. But the work has finally begun.

Twenty-six years later, Bruce uncovers a fortune his father had quietly set aside—seed money for a plan Thomas never finished. Bruce invests it, buys back a neglected mansion, and gives the work a public name: Wayne Enterprises.

From the outside, it looks like a return to the life he was born to lead. The grand rooms fill with donors, champagne, and polished promises. Harvey Dent, Gotham’s tireless district attorney, is among the guests. He believes the city can be repaired through courage and honest institutions.

Bruce admires that conviction. He also knows how many people are waiting for someone else to fix things. Behind the parties, he begins asking harder questions about what a single person can do.

'}, 105: {date:'GOTHAM CITY · 2009',title:'The cost of hope',text:'

A year later, a terrible incident leaves Harvey Dent’s face scarred and his life changed. The city’s bright public hope is suddenly vulnerable to pain, anger, and the cruel appetite of headlines. Bruce watches the damage from a distance and recognizes the same old feeling: the moment when safety proves it was never guaranteed.

He retreats from the parties and the easy explanations. With a bag in hand, he descends beneath Wayne Manor into a forgotten cave. The stone is cold, the passages are rough, and the darkness seems almost honest. Here, at least, nobody asks him to smile for a photograph.

For a while, Bruce tells himself solitude is the same thing as purpose.

'}, 106: {date:'WAYNE CAVE · THE FIRST VISIT',title:'A man in the dark',text:'

“Excuse me, sir. Are you looking for something?” an old man calls from the cave entrance. “There’s nothing in here. It’s old—just like me.”

Bruce bristles. “I’m trying to do something with this place. What makes you think you can tell me what to do?” The stranger does not rise to the challenge. He simply points out that Bruce is standing on private property and waits for him to answer.

Bruce refuses to leave. The old man gives him one last look and walks away. The exchange is awkward, almost absurd, but it stays with Bruce. Someone has finally spoken to him plainly, without fear of his name or his money.

'}, 107: {date:'WAYNE CAVE · THREE MONTHS LATER',title:'The long quiet',text:'

Days pass. Bruce returns to the cave with tools, then with plans, then with nothing but questions. He measures the cavern and marks out possible work areas. He tries to turn the rock into a headquarters by force of will, but every task exposes another one he does not know how to do.

Above him, the manor continues its routines. Below, the cave answers with drips of water and the occasional flutter of wings. Bruce begins to understand that a mission built alone may only become another way to hide.

One evening he hears footsteps at the entrance. The same old man has come back. This time, he is carrying a thermos and a small stack of notes.

'}, 108: {date:'WAYNE CAVE · A RETURN',title:'An unexpected ally',text:'

“Excuse me, sir. Remember me?” The man sets down the thermos. “I’m Alfred.” Bruce has known him all his life, of course, but down here they meet differently: not as employer and servant, nor as grieving boy and patient guardian, but as two people looking at the same unfinished room.

Alfred has sketched a workbench, a computer station, and a safer route back to the house. He has also found a book on self-defense. Bruce studies the pages and recognizes how much he does not know. Alfred does not gloat. He pours tea.

“You’ll need more than determination, sir,” he says. “Determination is what gets you to the door. Preparation is what gets you home.”

'}, 109: {date:'WAYNE CAVE · THE PLAN TAKES SHAPE',title:'Tools, not answers',text:'

They work in fits and starts. Alfred knows how to keep a project moving; Bruce knows how to ask questions that make the project bigger. The computer station becomes a place to sort reports and maps. A suit bay takes shape against the stone. The elevator connects the cave to the estate without sending either man through the front hall.

Every object has a purpose and a limit. Batarangs can distract or disarm, but they cannot make a bad decision wise. Smoke pellets can cover a retreat, but they cannot turn a retreat into a victory. A grapple prototype can bridge a gap only if the person using it thinks before leaping.

Bruce begins to see the cave not as a lair, but as a workshop for learning how to help.

'}, 110: {date:'WAYNE CAVE · THE VEHICLE BAY',title:'A machine with sharp edges',text:'

The car is the most ambitious piece of the plan and the least finished. Its armored panels catch the work lights; its engine answers a test with a growl that makes dust fall from the ceiling. Alfred circles it with a clipboard, noting what still needs attention.

“It’s not quite street legal,” he says. “And I would avoid the red switch.” Bruce asks if it is safe. Alfred considers the question for a beat too long. They agree to call it a prototype and to keep the first test somewhere far from traffic.

The machine represents possibility, but also temptation: the urge to make an entrance instead of doing the patient work. Bruce closes the hood. Tonight, the car can wait.

'}, 111: {date:'WAYNE CAVE · BEFORE DAWN',title:'The first lesson',text:'

Alfred lays the self-defense field guide on the workbench. It is not as impressive as the suit, the car, or the glowing computer screens. Its pages are worn at the corners, full of diagrams and notes in Alfred’s neat hand. Bruce opens it carefully.

“Begin with the book,” Alfred tells him. “Learn how to keep your balance. Learn when to move, when to listen, and when walking away is the bravest thing you can do.” Bruce looks toward the equipment waiting around the cave. For the first time, it feels less like a collection of answers and more like a list of responsibilities.

There is still a long way to go. But the work has finally begun.

'}, 112: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 01',title:'The first patrol',text:'

At 02:14, Bruce leaves the cave in the unfinished suit. The city is wet, violent, and divided into islands of light. Alfred watches on the radio, correcting course without pretending to know the way.

Bruce stops a mugging near Crime Alley. The victim asks why a masked man would help. Bruce answers that the city was not enough to save his parents, then recognizes that this is not the whole truth.

He returns before dawn. Alfred: “You survived. Tomorrow, we improve the plan.”

'}, 113: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 02',title:'The Red Triangle',text:'

A traveling circus van appears in four simultaneous theft reports. Children call the masked thieves acrobats. Alfred calls them organized. Batman calls them a warning.

A red-winged emblem leads to the Penguin. Oswald Cobblepot is buying sewer access, waterfront property, and the loyalty of Gotham’s hungry.

Batman closes the first vault, but Cobblepot escapes into the neglected flood tunnels beneath the East End.

'}, 114: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 04',title:'Riddles in rain',text:'

Green question marks appear across public records. The Riddler, Edward Nygma, claims Gotham’s hidden systems are puzzles waiting for a clever hand.

Every riddle names a witness. One points to Dent. Another points to Wayne Enterprises. Batman learns the difference between being mocked and being asked a question.

The latest challenge leads to the clocktower and a trap that nearly buries the Batmobile beneath glass and steel.

'}, 115: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 06',title:'The tea invitation',text:'

Poison Ivy has sealed an abandoned greenhouse beneath Robinson Park. Police drones wilt at the glass. Inside, Jervis Tetch—the Mad Hatter—hosts a tea party for captives whose memories have been altered by a mind-control device.

Ivy offers Batman a bargain: expose Wayne Enterprises’ toxic contracts, and she will free the hostages. He refuses to bargain with hostages, but accepts a smaller truth—Gotham poisoned the soil long before Ivy began fighting for it.

The tea party ends, though Tetch slips away through a maintenance door.

'}, 116: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 08',title:'Killer Croc below',text:'

During a subway evacuation, Killer Croc overturns a construction train. Batman finds the panic is real but the attack is scripted: the train carries stolen medical serum for Bane.

Croc could have escaped. Instead he remains to protect trapped maintenance workers. Batman recognizes manipulation, but not enough to release Croc without judgment.

Alfred extracts the workers. Croc disappears below the city, leaving a warning: “He knows where you sleep.”

'}, 117: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 10',title:'Red Hood',text:'

The Batcomputer identifies an unauthorized vigilante using a red hood and brutal methods. Witnesses call him Jason Todd. The name reaches Bruce before the evidence does.

Jason confronts Batman with a list of criminals he believes Batman is protecting by restraint. Their argument becomes a pursuit over the Narrows rooftops. Jason is faster, angrier, and less afraid to fall.

Batman loses sight of him. Alfred reminds Bruce that refusing to become a killer does not mean ignoring a former student in pain.

'}, 118: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 12',title:'The laughing dossier',text:'

The Joker infiltrates Gotham General disguised as an orderly. No one agrees on his motive because no one agrees on the crime: he steals blood, a birthday card, and a list of sealed witnesses.

Batman enters the hospital in a silence of IV pumps and humming machines. Joker leaves a riddle: “A city is a joke only when everyone forgets the punchline.”

Gordon finds Batman at the emergency stairwell. Together they realize the random incidents form a map.

'}, 119: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 14',title:'Beneath the courthouse',text:'

The villains’ crimes point toward a buried transit station beneath Gotham’s old courthouse. Bane controls it, but he has not moved against Batman directly.

He has assembled the city’s broken agents and given each a customized target. He calls it the Twenty-Four, because Gotham has been warned for too long.

Batman sees the larger plan: overwhelm the night, isolate Gordon, turn every hero into evidence, and reveal an exhausted city.

'}, 120: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 16',title:'Two-Face’s choice',text:'

Two-Face takes control of the abandoned 1st National vault. His decisions are determined by a scarred coin, but his speeches are never left to chance.

He offers Batman a seat in judgment: save one district attorney or one innocent witness. Batman instead saves both, but Dent refuses to recognize a victory without a rule.

Before he leaves, Dent warns Bruce that justice built on luck is still only fear wearing a uniform.

'}, 121: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 18',title:'The plant underground',text:'

Ivy turns Gotham’s pumping stations green. Trees break through asphalt and vines pull at sewer gates. The transformation could flood half the East End, but Ivy insists it is a quarantine.

Batman learns Wayne Enterprises used the aquifer for unauthorized waste storage. He cannot deny the evidence. He promises to open every record and resign his public defenses.

Ivy releases the city from the flood, on the condition that Alfred, not a corporation, manage the first cleanup.

'}, 122: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 20',title:'Cobblepot’s shadow',text:'

The Penguin activates his waterline fleet. Armed umbrellas become alarms and submarines masquerade as municipal barges. Cobblepot intends to make Gotham physically dependent on his monopoly.

Batman dismantles the barges with a blackout, then risks capture to stop a worker trapped below deck. Cobblepot is impressed and angry because the rescue undermines his story.

For the first time, the villain offers Batman a truce—of convenience.

'}, 123: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 22',title:'The Mad Hatter’s signal',text:'

Jervis Tetch broadcasts a hypnotic children’s program across Gotham. Everyone who watches begins repeating nursery rhymes and forgetting recent hours.

Batman and Gordon use a dead analog signal to reach the city’s radio engineers. Alfred reconstructs Tetch’s command pattern from a field of nonsense.

The broadcast ends. Tetch is arrested smiling, but he has not revealed the four-hour gap Bane required.

'}, 124: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 24',title:'The war in the halfway house',text:'

Jason Todd ambushes two rival gangs carrying Bane’s serum. One gang member recognizes Jason and calls him Robin, though Jason rejects the name. Batman finds the boy beneath the red hood just as Bane’s scouts arrive.

Bane breaks through the ceiling and defeats Batman with precise force. Jason saves him, not out of forgiveness, but because Bane did not grant anyone a choice.

For the first time, Batman understands Jason may be his ally rather than his opposite.

'}, 125: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 26',title:'A board vote',text:'

Lucius Fox brings Bruce evidence of a Wayne Enterprises board plot. The villains have bought influence through companies hidden behind the aquifer scandal.

Bruce returns to a boardroom, shedding the Batman persona instead of hiding behind it. He releases the corruption files, cancels failed programs, and offers workers amnesty for testimony.

It is a political victory—and a public target. Joker sends Bruce a photograph of Wayne Manor with the lights still on.

## Objective
- Improve the playable game’s movement and expand its story, visuals, and villain roster.

## Requirements
- Make the story long: 40 chapters and 40 hours.
- Add Batman and face visuals, and include Bane, Mad Hatter, the Riddler, Joker, Two-Face, Penguin, Killer Croc, Jason Todd, and Poison Ivy.
- Save verification screenshots as JPEGs no wider than 1280px, and inspect only the latest screenshot.

## Decisions
- Use boolean key states for movement so missing keys cannot produce `NaN`.
- Raise the frame delta-time cap for better responsiveness during slow frames.
- Keep the 12-beat story and scrollable story card; disable renderer shadows and lower pixel ratio. These decisions predate and may conflict with the newer 40-chapter request.

## Work State
### Completed
- Fixed keyboard movement and removed temporary debug hooks in `index.html`.
- Verified story progression, keyboard movement, and equipment interaction with Playwright.
- Passed JavaScript syntax checking and `git diff --check`; browser console reported no errors or warnings.
- Captured and inspected `screenshots/wayne-latest.jpg` at 1280×800.

### Active
- Update the story to 40 chapters and 40 hours, add Batman’s face/visuals, and incorporate the requested villains.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect the current `index.html` and implement the requested story, character visuals, and villain roster.
2. Verify the game and capture/inspect the latest compliant JPEG screenshot.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Game story, controls, rendering, and movement logic.
- `screenshots/wayne-latest.jpg`: Latest inspected verification screenshot.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted; `index.html` was modified at the last recorded status check.

Gotham’s old theater empties into a rain-bright street. Thomas and Martha Wayne walk home with their young son, Bruce, still talking about the film. His mother holds his hand; his father listens as if the story matters as much as the night is beautiful.

Their shortcut passes a narrow alley. A stranger steps from the dark and asks for money. Thomas gives the gunman $200—everything he has—and tries to make himself the only danger in the alley.

“Take it. Just let my family go.”

For one suspended second, the city seems to hold its breath.

'}, 102: {date:'GOTHAM CITY · THAT NIGHT',title:'The promise',text:'

The gunshot cracks across the street. Thomas and Martha fall beneath the streetlamp. Bruce is left kneeling beside them, surrounded by a city that keeps moving but will never look the same to him again.

In the weeks that follow, adults speak softly around him. They tell him he is safe now, that the police will find the killer, that time will make the pain smaller. None of those words can bring his parents back. Bruce learns that helplessness can feel louder than any siren.

Grief hardens into a promise—not a plan yet, only a vow he will carry into every room: no one else should have to feel this alone.

'}, 103: {date:'WAYNE MANOR · THE YEARS AFTER',title:'A house full of echoes',text:'

The manor is enormous, but after the funeral it feels too quiet. Bruce grows up among portraits, locked rooms, and the careful kindness of the family’s longtime butler, Alfred Pennyworth. Alfred makes breakfast, remembers birthdays, and never asks Bruce to pretend he is all right.

Bruce studies, travels, and searches for a way to understand the violence that took his parents. He learns how fear works, how people survive, and how easily a powerful family can mistake its own comfort for the health of its city.

The promise stays with him. It changes shape as he does: first a child’s wish, then a question, and finally a responsibility he cannot hand to anyone else.

'}, 104: {date:'GOTHAM CITY · 2008',title:'A fortune, a house, a name',text:'

Twenty-six years later, Bruce uncovers a fortune his father had quietly set aside—seed money for a plan Thomas never finished. Bruce invests it, buys back a neglected mansion, and gives the work a public name: Wayne Enterprises.

From the outside, it looks like a return to the life he was born to lead. The grand rooms fill with donors, champagne, and polished promises. Harvey Dent, Gotham’s tireless district attorney, is among the guests. He believes the city can be repaired through courage and honest institutions.

Bruce admires that conviction. He also knows how many people are waiting for someone else to fix things. Behind the parties, he begins asking harder questions about what a single person can do.

'}, 105: {date:'GOTHAM CITY · 2009',title:'The cost of hope',text:'

A year later, a terrible incident leaves Harvey Dent’s face scarred and his life changed. The city’s bright public hope is suddenly vulnerable to pain, anger, and the cruel appetite of headlines. Bruce watches the damage from a distance and recognizes the same old feeling: the moment when safety proves it was never guaranteed.

He retreats from the parties and the easy explanations. With a bag in hand, he descends beneath Wayne Manor into a forgotten cave. The stone is cold, the passages are rough, and the darkness seems almost honest. Here, at least, nobody asks him to smile for a photograph.

For a while, Bruce tells himself solitude is the same thing as purpose.

'}, 106: {date:'WAYNE CAVE · THE FIRST VISIT',title:'A man in the dark',text:'

“Excuse me, sir. Are you looking for something?” an old man calls from the cave entrance. “There’s nothing in here. It’s old—just like me.”

Bruce bristles. “I’m trying to do something with this place. What makes you think you can tell me what to do?” The stranger does not rise to the challenge. He simply points out that Bruce is standing on private property and waits for him to answer.

Bruce refuses to leave. The old man gives him one last look and walks away. The exchange is awkward, almost absurd, but it stays with Bruce. Someone has finally spoken to him plainly, without fear of his name or his money.

'}, 107: {date:'WAYNE CAVE · THREE MONTHS LATER',title:'The long quiet',text:'

Days pass. Bruce returns to the cave with tools, then with plans, then with nothing but questions. He measures the cavern and marks out possible work areas. He tries to turn the rock into a headquarters by force of will, but every task exposes another one he does not know how to do.

Above him, the manor continues its routines. Below, the cave answers with drips of water and the occasional flutter of wings. Bruce begins to understand that a mission built alone may only become another way to hide.

One evening he hears footsteps at the entrance. The same old man has come back. This time, he is carrying a thermos and a small stack of notes.

'}, 108: {date:'WAYNE CAVE · A RETURN',title:'An unexpected ally',text:'

“Excuse me, sir. Remember me?” The man sets down the thermos. “I’m Alfred.” Bruce has known him all his life, of course, but down here they meet differently: not as employer and servant, nor as grieving boy and patient guardian, but as two people looking at the same unfinished room.

Alfred has sketched a workbench, a computer station, and a safer route back to the house. He has also found a book on self-defense. Bruce studies the pages and recognizes how much he does not know. Alfred does not gloat. He pours tea.

“You’ll need more than determination, sir,” he says. “Determination is what gets you to the door. Preparation is what gets you home.”

'}, 109: {date:'WAYNE CAVE · THE PLAN TAKES SHAPE',title:'Tools, not answers',text:'

They work in fits and starts. Alfred knows how to keep a project moving; Bruce knows how to ask questions that make the project bigger. The computer station becomes a place to sort reports and maps. A suit bay takes shape against the stone. The elevator connects the cave to the estate without sending either man through the front hall.

Every object has a purpose and a limit. Batarangs can distract or disarm, but they cannot make a bad decision wise. Smoke pellets can cover a retreat, but they cannot turn a retreat into a victory. A grapple prototype can bridge a gap only if the person using it thinks before leaping.

Bruce begins to see the cave not as a lair, but as a workshop for learning how to help.

'}, 110: {date:'WAYNE CAVE · THE VEHICLE BAY',title:'A machine with sharp edges',text:'

The car is the most ambitious piece of the plan and the least finished. Its armored panels catch the work lights; its engine answers a test with a growl that makes dust fall from the ceiling. Alfred circles it with a clipboard, noting what still needs attention.

“It’s not quite street legal,” he says. “And I would avoid the red switch.” Bruce asks if it is safe. Alfred considers the question for a beat too long. They agree to call it a prototype and to keep the first test somewhere far from traffic.

The machine represents possibility, but also temptation: the urge to make an entrance instead of doing the patient work. Bruce closes the hood. Tonight, the car can wait.

'}, 111: {date:'WAYNE CAVE · BEFORE DAWN',title:'The first lesson',text:'

Alfred lays the self-defense field guide on the workbench. It is not as impressive as the suit, the car, or the glowing computer screens. Its pages are worn at the corners, full of diagrams and notes in Alfred’s neat hand. Bruce opens it carefully.

“Begin with the book,” Alfred tells him. “Learn how to keep your balance. Learn when to move, when to listen, and when walking away is the bravest thing you can do.” Bruce looks toward the equipment waiting around the cave. For the first time, it feels less like a collection of answers and more like a list of responsibilities.

There is still a long way to go. But the work has finally begun.

'}, 112: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 01',title:'The first patrol',text:'

At 02:14, Bruce leaves the cave in the unfinished suit. The city is wet, violent, and divided into islands of light. Alfred watches on the radio, correcting course without pretending to know the way.

Bruce stops a mugging near Crime Alley. The victim asks why a masked man would help. Bruce answers that the city was not enough to save his parents, then recognizes that this is not the whole truth.

He returns before dawn. Alfred: “You survived. Tomorrow, we improve the plan.”

'}, 113: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 02',title:'The Red Triangle',text:'

A traveling circus van appears in four simultaneous theft reports. Children call the masked thieves acrobats. Alfred calls them organized. Batman calls them a warning.

A red-winged emblem leads to the Penguin. Oswald Cobblepot is buying sewer access, waterfront property, and the loyalty of Gotham’s hungry.

Batman closes the first vault, but Cobblepot escapes into the neglected flood tunnels beneath the East End.

'}, 114: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 03',title:'The umbrella maps',text:'

Batman follows the Penguin through a museum gala. Cobblepot expects fear and receives documentation: warehouse manifests, bribed inspectors, and the names of families paid to disappear.

Alfred finds a pattern in the stolen city maps. The Penguin is not building one escape route. He is buying every exit Gotham still has.

Batman leaves the gala with a warning for Gordon and one umbrella embedded in the Batmobile’s radiator.

'}, 115: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 04',title:'Riddles in rain',text:'

Green question marks appear across public records. The Riddler, Edward Nygma, claims Gotham’s hidden systems are puzzles waiting for a clever hand.

Every riddle names a witness. One points to Dent. Another points to Wayne Enterprises. Batman learns the difference between being mocked and being asked a question.

The latest challenge leads to the clocktower and a trap that nearly buries the Batmobile beneath glass and steel.

'}, 116: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 05',title:'The question of mercy',text:'

Nygma captures a Wayne Enterprises audit team inside the clocktower. The first question asks Batman to identify a corrupt name. The second asks whether exposing it will save the workers beside it.

Batman refuses the game long enough to answer both. He sends Gordon the list and lowers the team by cable. Nygma is furious that the puzzle solved itself.

Yet a message remains: the Riddler has been hired to find Gotham’s hidden witnesses.

'}, 117: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 06',title:'The tea invitation',text:'

Poison Ivy has sealed an abandoned greenhouse beneath Robinson Park. Police drones wilt at the glass. Inside, Jervis Tetch—the Mad Hatter—hosts a tea party for captives whose memories have been altered by a mind-control device.

Ivy offers Batman a bargain: expose Wayne Enterprises’ toxic contracts, and she will free the hostages. He refuses to bargain with hostages, but accepts a smaller truth—Gotham poisoned the soil long before Ivy began fighting for it.

The tea party ends, though Tetch slips away through a maintenance door.

'}, 118: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 08',title:'Killer Croc below',text:'

During a subway evacuation, Killer Croc overturns a construction train. Batman finds the panic is real but the attack is scripted: the train carries stolen medical serum for Bane.

Croc could have escaped. Instead he remains to protect trapped maintenance workers. Batman recognizes manipulation, but not enough to release Croc without judgment.

Alfred extracts the workers. Croc disappears below the city, leaving a warning: “He knows where you sleep.”

'}, 119: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 10',title:'Red Hood',text:'

The Batcomputer identifies an unauthorized vigilante using a red hood and brutal methods. Witnesses call him Jason Todd. The name reaches Bruce before the evidence does.

Jason confronts Batman with a list of criminals he believes Batman is protecting by restraint. Their argument becomes a pursuit over the Narrows rooftops. Jason is faster, angrier, and less afraid to fall.

Batman loses sight of him. Alfred reminds Bruce that refusing to become a killer does not mean ignoring a former student in pain.

'}, 120: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 12',title:'The laughing dossier',text:'

The Joker infiltrates Gotham General disguised as an orderly. No one agrees on his motive because no one agrees on the crime: he steals blood, a birthday card, and a list of sealed witnesses.

Batman enters the hospital in a silence of IV pumps and humming machines. Joker leaves a riddle: “A city is a joke only when everyone forgets the punchline.”

Gordon finds Batman at the emergency stairwell. Together they realize the random incidents form a map.

'}, 121: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 14',title:'Beneath the courthouse',text:'

The villains’ crimes point toward a buried transit station beneath Gotham’s old courthouse. Bane controls it, but he has not moved against Batman directly.

He has assembled the city’s broken agents and given each a customized target. He calls it the Twenty-Four, because Gotham has been warned for too long.

Batman sees the larger plan: overwhelm the night, isolate Gordon, turn every hero into evidence, and reveal an exhausted city.

'}, 122: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 16',title:'Two-Face’s choice',text:'

Two-Face takes control of the abandoned 1st National vault. His decisions are determined by a scarred coin, but his speeches are never left to chance.

He offers Batman a seat in judgment: save one district attorney or one innocent witness. Batman instead saves both, but Dent refuses to recognize a victory without a rule.

Before he leaves, Dent warns Bruce that justice built on luck is still only fear wearing a uniform.

'}, 123: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 18',title:'The plant underground',text:'

Ivy turns Gotham’s pumping stations green. Trees break through asphalt and vines pull at sewer gates. The transformation could flood half the East End, but Ivy insists it is a quarantine.

Batman learns Wayne Enterprises used the aquifer for unauthorized waste storage. He cannot deny the evidence. He promises to open every record and resign his public defenses.

Ivy releases the city from the flood, on the condition that Alfred, not a corporation, manage the first cleanup.

'}, 124: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 20',title:'Cobblepot’s shadow',text:'

The Penguin activates his waterline fleet. Armed umbrellas become alarms and submarines masquerade as municipal barges. Cobblepot intends to make Gotham physically dependent on his monopoly.

Batman dismantles the barges with a blackout, then risks capture to stop a worker trapped below deck. Cobblepot is impressed and angry because the rescue undermines his story.

For the first time, the villain offers Batman a truce—of convenience.

'}, 125: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 22',title:'The Mad Hatter’s signal',text:'

Jervis Tetch broadcasts a hypnotic children’s program across Gotham. Everyone who watches begins repeating nursery rhymes and forgetting recent hours.

Batman and Gordon use a dead analog signal to reach the city’s radio engineers. Alfred reconstructs Tetch’s command pattern from a field of nonsense.

The broadcast ends. Tetch is arrested smiling, but he has not revealed the four-hour gap Bane required.

'}, 126: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 24',title:'The war in the halfway house',text:'

Jason Todd ambushes two rival gangs carrying Bane’s serum. One gang member recognizes Jason and calls him Robin, though Jason rejects the name. Batman finds the boy beneath the red hood just as Bane’s scouts arrive.

Bane breaks through the ceiling and defeats Batman with precise force. Jason saves him, not out of forgiveness, but because Bane did not grant anyone a choice.

For the first time, Batman understands Jason may be his ally rather than his opposite.

'}, 127: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 26',title:'A board vote',text:'

Lucius Fox brings Bruce evidence of a Wayne Enterprises board plot. The villains have bought influence through companies hidden behind the aquifer scandal.

Bruce returns to a boardroom, shedding the Batman persona instead of hiding behind it. He releases the corruption files, cancels failed programs, and offers workers amnesty for testimony.

It is a political victory—and a public target. Joker sends Bruce a photograph of Wayne Manor with the lights still on.

'}, 128: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 28',title:'Killer Croc in daylight',text:'

Killer Croc emerges from the canal to deliver Bane’s ledger to Gordon. He was never loyal to Bane; he was protecting sewer workers forced into labor.

Batman must decide whether to arrest Croc or accept his evidence. Gordon gives the decision to Croc’s people. They choose the witness interview.

Alfred calls it a legal inconvenience. Bruce calls it the beginning of a neighborhood becoming visible.

'}, 129: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 30',title:'The trap in the sky',text:'

Nygma takes control of the GCPD light grid and paints questions across Gotham’s clouds. Each correct answer disables a bomb. The puzzle is not in logic but in sacrifice: each answer protects a district he has already abandoned.

Batman realizes Nygma expects him to save the district where Wayne Enterprises began. He chooses the poorest district instead. The explosives expose a hidden tunnel rather than a skyline.

Nygma escapes into Arkham’s east wing, laughing that Batman solved the wrong problem first.

'}, 130: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 32',title:'Arkham without walls',text:'

Arkham’s east wing is opened, not breached. Two-Face, Joker, Ivy, Nygma, and Cobblepot have their own exits. Bane planned to give Gotham a choice: submit or chase.

Batman refuses to pursue every criminal at once. Gordon organizes the city, Jason handles one street gang, and Ivy frees patients from Tetch’s signal.

The first true alliance begins without costumes or speeches. Alfred arranges for coffee and batteries.

'}, 131: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 34',title:'The coin falls',text:'

Two-Face arrives in the Arkham chapel. Dent demands a final vote on Batman’s future. Gordon presents evidence that Dent was manipulated as carefully as every other villain.

For once, Dent cannot blame chance. He flips the coin and refuses the result, splitting it across the chapel floor.

Batman and Gordon escort him to trial. Dent looks almost relieved to be answered by a law he can challenge rather than chance that cannot hear him.

'}, 132: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 36',title:'The Lazarus engine',text:'

Bane activates machinery beneath Gotham to flood the storm drains and isolate the Narrows. His goal is not destruction; it is to force Batman to choose between the wealthy and the poor.

Batman shuts down the engine from three locations, aided by the criminals who now know Bane lied to them. Croc removes a jammed gate. Ivy restores the plant relays. Jason saves the control team.

Bane remains in the center of the storm, waiting for Batman to become afraid enough to fight alone.

'}, 133: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 38',title:'The silent promise',text:'

Joker has rigged Wayne Manor’s cave elevator with a trap. Batman enters believing Alfred is trapped inside. Instead Alfred is still at the manor, guiding a civilian evacuation.

The Joker appears on every monitor. “No mask,” he says, “no miracle.” Batman answers in Bruce Wayne’s voice: there is no miracle, only a team that can survive the next minute.

Joker loses interest in a man who cannot be reduced to a single reaction. He escapes toward Bane’s citadel.

'}, 134: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 39',title:'The last enemy',text:'

Bane offers Batman the city in exchange for surrendering the Batcave. All Gotham must do is kneel, Bane says, and he will stop breaking it.

Batman refuses. Alfred, Gordon, Jason, Fox, Croc, Ivy, Dent, and the Penguin’s former workers link into a plan spanning streets, towers, tunnels, and servers.

Bane calls them a crowd. Batman calls them Gotham.

'}, 135: {date:'GOTHAM · HOUR 40',title:'Forty hours until dawn',text:'

At the end of forty hours, Batman faces Bane above the flooded central square. He does not win because he is stronger. He wins because preparation has turned every lesson into a choice.

Jason prevents a collapse. Gordon opens the escape routes. Ivy disables the venom pumps. Croc removes Bane’s final supports. Dent and Cobblepot choose their own codes of justice. Joker, Nygma, and Tetch are confined where they cannot direct the city.

Dawn reaches Wayne Tower. Bruce watches with Alfred and knows the promise is not to end fear. It is to keep working until every frightened person can come home.

The first night became forty hours. Gotham remained. So did the work.

'}, [Output truncated. Continue reading with offset: 136]

## Objective
- Improve the playable game’s movement and expand its story, visuals, and villain roster.

## Requirements
- Make the story 40 chapters and 40 hours.
- Add Batman and face visuals, and include Bane, Mad Hatter, the Riddler, Joker, Two-Face, Penguin, Killer Croc, Jason Todd, and Poison Ivy.
- Save verification screenshots as JPEGs no wider than 1280px, and inspect only the latest screenshot.

## Decisions
- Use boolean key states for movement so missing keys cannot produce `NaN`.
- Raise the frame delta-time cap for better responsiveness during slow frames.
- Keep the 12-beat story and scrollable story card; disable renderer shadows and lower pixel ratio. These earlier decisions may conflict with the newer 40-chapter request.

## Work State
### Completed
- Fixed keyboard movement and removed temporary debug hooks in `index.html`.
- Verified story progression, keyboard movement, and equipment interaction with Playwright.
- Passed JavaScript syntax checking and `git diff --check` in earlier verification.
- Captured and inspected `screenshots/wayne-latest.jpg` at 1280×800.
- Replaced most of the original story array with an expanded Batman campaign and added Hour 03 and Hour 05 entries.

### Active
- Complete the story to 40 chapters/hours; the latest count was 36 scenes, including the cave finale.
- Add or verify Batman and face visuals.
- Verify all requested villains are included and the game still works.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Add the remaining four story scenes; then verify the campaign count and hour labels.
2. Inspect and update character/face visuals and confirm the villain roster.
3. Validate JavaScript using the actual script-tag format, run browser checks, capture a compliant latest JPEG, and inspect only that screenshot.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Story array, game visuals, controls, rendering, and movement.
- `screenshots/wayne-latest.jpg`: Previously inspected verification screenshot.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted.
- The latest story count was 36 scenes; the prior plan was to add Hours 07, 09, 11, and 13.
- A syntax-check attempt failed because it searched for a literal `<script>` tag and reported `script missing`; the correct script extraction is unresolved.
- `git diff --check` passed after the story replacement, before the latest additions.
